facts.title: The Stranger Among Gases
facts.text: Xenon was discovered in 1898 by Scottish chemist William Ramsay and English chemist Morris Travers, who found it as a tiny residue left after evaporating liquefied air. Its name comes from the Greek word 'xenos', meaning stranger or foreigner, because it appeared so unexpectedly and in such minuscule amounts. The same pair had already isolated neon and krypton from air just weeks earlier.

facts.title: Vanishingly Rare in Our Air
facts.text: Despite being all around us, xenon makes up only about 0.087 parts per million of Earth's atmosphere, roughly one part in 11.5 million by volume. To collect it, industrial plants must liquefy enormous quantities of air and separate the components by fractional distillation. This rarity is a big reason xenon is one of the more expensive gases to buy.

facts.title: It Breaks the Noble Rules
facts.text: For decades chemists believed the noble gases were completely inert and could form no compounds at all. In 1962 Neil Bartlett at the University of British Columbia shattered that idea by making xenon hexafluoroplatinate, the first real noble-gas compound. Today many xenon compounds are known, including xenon tetrafluoride and the dangerously explosive xenon trioxide.

facts.title: Light of the Movie Projector
facts.text: When electricity passes through xenon, it produces a brilliant white light whose spectrum closely matches natural daylight. Xenon arc lamps power cinema projectors, searchlights, and high-end car headlights, and they were once used in IMAX projectors drawing thousands of watts. The familiar burst of a camera flash also comes from a brief, intense electrical discharge through xenon gas.

facts.title: An Anesthetic Noble Gas
facts.text: Breathing xenon can render a person unconscious, and it works as a genuine general anesthetic by blocking certain receptors in the brain. It is prized in medicine because it acts quickly, wears off fast, and protects nerve cells, with very few side effects on the heart and circulation. Its high cost, however, keeps it from being used in everyday surgery.

facts.title: A Voice Deeper Than Helium
facts.text: Helium famously makes your voice squeaky, but xenon does the opposite because it is far denser than air. Sound travels more slowly through the heavy gas, lowering the pitch of your voice to a comical growl. Inhaling it is genuinely dangerous, though, since xenon can displace oxygen in the lungs and cause suffocation.

facts.title: Fuel for Spacecraft Engines
facts.text: Xenon is the propellant of choice for ion thrusters, the gentle but highly efficient engines used on deep-space probes. NASA's Dawn mission to the asteroids Vesta and Ceres carried over 400 kilograms of xenon, accelerating its ions to push the craft for years. These engines sip fuel so frugally that they can run almost continuously for the entire voyage.

facts.title: A Clock Inside the Earth
facts.text: Some xenon in nature is radiogenic, meaning it formed from the radioactive decay of other elements over billions of years. Xenon-129 comes from extinct iodine-129, and xenon-136 from the incredibly slow double beta decay of itself, used in rare experiments hunting for neutrino properties. Scientists read these xenon 'fingerprints' to date events from the early solar system.

facts.title: Hunting for Dark Matter
facts.text: Several of the world's most sensitive dark-matter detectors are giant tanks filled with liquid xenon kept colder than minus 100 degrees Celsius. Experiments like LUX-ZEPLIN and XENONnT watch for the faint flash and charge that a passing dark-matter particle might produce when it strikes a xenon nucleus. Xenon's heavy nucleus and self-shielding purity make it ideal for spotting such whisper-quiet events.

facts.title: Glowing Lungs on a Scan
facts.text: A special version of xenon, the isotope xenon-129, can be 'hyperpolarized' with lasers so its tiny magnetic signal becomes thousands of times stronger. Patients inhale this gas and an MRI scanner then maps how air flows into every corner of the lungs in real time. This lets doctors see lung diseases like asthma and COPD without any X-rays or radiation.
